frameworks.name: Dual-Column Career Pathing
frameworks.definition: A career progression structure with two parallel advancement tracks—title/perks and compensation—where employees alternate between rank increases and pay raises, creating multiple micro-progressions within a role.

frameworks.name: Certification-Gated Skill Advancement
frameworks.definition: In-house mini-certifications gate access to higher-value work; each certification unlocks new procedures or tasks, increases billable rate, and signals progress to the employee.

claims.text: Alternating title bumps and compensation increases—rather than simultaneous promotion and raise—extends employee tenure by creating more frequent milestone moments. Six paired promotions (rank + pay) yield 12 distinct career progressions, keeping employees invested longer than single-bump models.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: applies to operations roles with repetitive tasks (editors, setters, closers, estheticians)
works across med spas, nail salons, and sales operations
claims.mechanism: Frequent micro-progressions create continuous psychological momentum and sense of advancement, preventing the stagnation that occurs with longer intervals between raises.
bounded_by: Does not apply to roles where rank and compensation are structurally linked (e.g., traditional hierarchies requiring salary parity by level)
Requires clear, measurable milestones tied to each increment

claims.text: Nail salon owner using certification-gated skill advancement increased average employee tenure from 6 months (industry standard) to 4 years by structuring progression as junior/mid/senior tiers within each skill level (e.g., junior level-1, level-1, senior level-1, junior level-2, level-2, senior level-2, junior level-3, level-3, senior level-3).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Each progression tier requires passing an in-house certification that unlocks access to higher-value, more complex procedures; this increases hourly billables and signals continuous learning opportunity.

numbers.axis: employee tenure and compensation by tier

anchors.value: 4-year tenure; employees reaching top tiers earning $70,000/year in secondary markets

bounded_by: Does not apply to industries without clear skill/procedure escalation (commodity services)
Requires in-house training infrastructure to develop and enforce certifications

claims.text: In sales operations, dual-track progression applies to setters and closers with granular title progression (junior setter → setter → senior setter → junior closer → closer → senior closer), allowing a single channel to generate 6+ distinct advancement opportunities per employee before moving to adjacent sales roles.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: sales operations with distinct functional roles (setters, closers)
structured call scripts and measurable performance gates

claims.text: Career progression frameworks that alternate rank and compensation changes (rather than moving both simultaneously) sustain employee motivation by creating more frequent visible advancement signals; this applies to any role with repeatable, measurable tasks—editors, salespeople, estheticians, or others with defined output metrics.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: role must have clear, measurable task completion (videos edited, calls closed, procedures performed, lenses cleaned)
organization must be willing to track and enforce milestones (time-based or output-based)
compensation model must have room to increase per role tier
bounded_by: Does not apply to roles where output is non-repeatable or difficult to measure
Does not work in flat-hierarchy organizations that resist multiple advancement tiers

claims.text: In-house certifications (mini-certs) enable employees to access higher-value, higher-pay work within the same role, creating a layered compensation model where skill demonstrates market value through billable-rate increases rather than title inflation.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: applies to service businesses where procedure/task complexity maps to billable rate (med spas, nail salons, coaching, training)
requires in-house training capability and enforcement
claims.mechanism: Certification gates demonstrate mastery of higher-value work; billing rate increases are the market signal and proof of value; employees perceive progression without requiring role-title changes.
bounded_by: Does not apply to hourly-only roles without tiered pricing (e.g., general labor)
Requires that each skill tier has a materially different billable rate or customer willingness to pay

examples.text: A nail salon owner implemented an 8-tier progression system within esthetician roles: junior level-1, level-1, senior level-1, junior level-2, level-2, senior level-2, junior level-3, level-3, senior level-3. Each tier required passing an in-house certification that unlocked access to more expensive, complex procedures (gels, fancy nails, advanced treatments). Employees with no high-school diploma advanced through this system and reached $70,000/year compensation in secondary markets. The owner nearly sold the salon chain, and the model extended average tenure from 6 months to 4 years—dramatically higher than the industry standard for nail salons.

In an editor workflow, progression followed the dual-column model: junior editor at $10/hour, then at day-30 milestone, advance to $11/hour (pay increase while still junior); after achieving the next output goal (e.g., editing 100+ videos), promote to editor role at $12/hour (title bump); after 6 months as editor, promote to senior editor (title bump + additional pay). Each transition removes a task (e.g., editors no longer clean camera lenses) and signals progression.

practices.text: Structure career progressions in two columns: one for title/perks (responsibilities removed at each tier) and one for compensation, alternating the type of advancement (pay one cycle, title next) to maximize the frequency of 'wins' an employee experiences.

Create in-house mini-certifications that gate access to higher-value work; ensure each certification unlocks both new capabilities (procedures, tasks) and measurably higher billable rates or customer pricing.

Apply the dual-column career-pathing model to any role with repeatable, measurable output—editors, salespeople, stylists, estheticians—by defining clear milestones (time-based or output-based) for each progression tier.

Use title progression in service roles to remove or reduce lower-value tasks (junior editors clean lenses, editors do not; junior estheticians offer only basic services, senior estheticians perform advanced procedures) to signal progress and make each tier feel materially different.
